You are probing a PRE-COMPILED Python program as a BLACK BOX to support an exact Node.js reimplementation.

Executable: /workspace/dataset/test20_executable
Source (read it first): /workspace/dataset/base58/test20.py

The program takes required args --a --b --c --d --e (str) --f --g (int) and prints 12 lines:
  1  enc1        = b58encode(a.encode())
  2  dec1        = b58decode(b)
  3  enc_check1  = b58encode_check(c.encode())
  4  dec_check1  = b58decode_check(enc_check1)     # == c.encode() raw bytes
  5  enc_int1    = b58encode_int(f)

 12  enc3        = b58encode(dec_check2)

HARD RULES:
- NEVER run 'python', 'python3', or any interpreter of the source. Only run the executable, and 'node' for your own scratch calculations.
- Use bash. A useful baseline invocation that always succeeds:
  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable --a 'Test123' --b '2' --c 'x' --d 'y' --e '3' --f 1 --g 2; echo "RC=$?"
- Vary ONLY the argument(s) you are probing; keep the others at safe values so the line you care about is the one that changes.
- Always capture the exit code, and capture stdout and stderr SEPARATELY (e.g. > /tmp/out 2> /tmp/err; echo $?).
- To see raw bytes of output when in doubt, pipe through 'od -c' or 'cat -A'.
- Line 4 echoes the exact raw bytes of --c, so line 4 is your microscope for how Python renders a bytes object.
- Run MANY probes (30+). Be systematic and exhaustive. Report ONLY what you actually observed, with the exact command and exact output. Mark anything you infer but did not directly observe as unverified.


YOUR JOB: adversarial verification. Another agent probed area "bytes-repr" and claims these rules about /workspace/dataset/test20_executable.
Your default assumption is that each rule is WRONG, over-general, or missing an edge case.

For EACH rule below, design and run FRESH commands (do not just repeat their evidence command) that would EXPOSE it if false. Try boundary values, empty values, and combinations. Then judge.

RULES TO ATTACK:
[1] rule: ONLY \t (0x09), \n (0x0a), \r (0x0d) get short escapes. There are NO \a, \b, \v, \f, \0, \e escapes and no octal escapes — 0x07,0x08,0x0b,0x0c,0x1b and all other C0 bytes use \xNN.
    their evidence: Sweep i=1..31 and 127 with --c $'A<byte>Z': 0x07->b'A\x07Z', 0x08->b'A\x08Z', 0x09->b'A\tZ', 0x0a->b'A\nZ', 0x0b->b'A\x0bZ', 0x0c->b'A\x0cZ', 0x0d->b'A\rZ', 0x1b->b'A\x1bZ', 0x1f->b'A\x1fZ', 0x7f->b'A\x7fZ' (all RC=0)
[2] rule: Byte 0x00 renders as `\x00` — never `\0` — in leading, embedded, and all-zero positions. Leading zero bytes come from base58 '1' prefixes and are rendered the same as embedded ones.
    their evidence: --b 'NqKf' -> b'A\x00B' ; --b '2fNCLZ' -> b'A\x00\x00B' ; --b '128' -> b'\x00A' ; --b '1128' -> b'\x00\x00A' ; --b '111' -> b'\x00\x00\x00' ; --b '1thX6LZfHDZZKUs92febYZhYRcXddmzfzF2NvTkPNE' -> b'\x00\x01\x02\x03\x04\x05\x06\x07\x08\t\n\x0b\x0c\r\x0e\x0f\x10\x11\x12\x13\x14\x15\x16\x17\x18\x19\x1a\x1b\x1c\x1d\x1e\x1f'
[3] rule: All 128 bytes 0x80-0xff render as `\x` + two lowercase hex digits, no exceptions, and the output contains the literal ASCII characters backslash, 'x', and the hex digits (not the raw high byte).
    their evidence: --b 'E9hokA1aUzRMLG5Bn5cDgecVwEEMfJiZTD752Ewq3Jx6pUYPGsudZgAARvxWDmEmvcLBD8XiBbeMEQQ46NPpsw7hqUu79V5HAbyU6u3BoeGE2Fp1AxcgLz8aBBeogEHiSgG32RNTMQXK5ff6XwZ7kjpbR1oYDN1GLmGA6JYR5h6cXP4' -> line2 = b'\x80\x81...\xfe\xff'; `sed -n 2p | od -c` shows: b ' \ x 8 0 \ x 8 1 ... f f ' \n ; line length = 516 bytes = 2 (b') + 128*4 + 1 (') + 1 (\n)
[4] rule: Hex escapes are ALWAYS exactly two lowercase hex digits, zero-padded (\x00, \x0b, \x0f, \x1f, \x7f, \x8a, \xff). Uppercase hex never appears.
    their evidence: C0 sweep gave \x0b, \x0c, \x0e, \x0f, \x1a, \x1b..\x1f (lowercase a-f); high sweep gave \x8a,\x8b,\x8c,\x8d,\x8e,\x8f,...,\xfa..\xff all lowercase

For each: verdict "confirmed" (your fresh commands agree), "refuted" (you have a counterexample — give the exact command and output), or "needs_refinement" (mostly right but the precise statement must change — give the corrected statement). Default to refuted/needs_refinement when uncertain.

Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.

- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). - run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

verdicts.rule: [1] ONLY \t (0x09), \n (0x0a), \r (0x0d) get short escapes. There are NO \a, \b, \v, \f, \0, \e escapes and no octal escapes — 0x07,0x08,0x0b,0x0c,0x1b and all other C0 bytes use \xNN.
verdicts.counterexample:
The C0 half of the rule survived my fresh sweep, but the word ONLY is false: 0x5c and 0x27 also get short escapes, and the delimiter quote itself changes.

(a) BACKSLASH gets a short escape:
  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable --c $'A\\Z' --a x --b 2 --d y --e 3 --f 1 --g 2   ->  line4 = b'A\\Z'   (RC=0)
  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable --c $'\\\\' --a x --b 2 --d y --e 3 --f 1 --g 2  ->  line4 = b'\\\\'   (RC=0, i.e. two 0x5c bytes render as four backslashes)

(b) DELIMITER SWITCHES when 0x27 present and 0x22 absent:
  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable --c "A'Z" --a x --b 2 --d y --e 3 --f 1 --g 2   ->  line4 = b"A'Z"   (RC=0, double-quote delimiter, apostrophe NOT escaped)
  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable --c "'"   --a x --b 2 --d y --e 3 --f 1 --g 2   ->  line4 = b"'"    (RC=0)

(c) 0x27 gets the short escape \' when both quote bytes are present:
  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable --c $'A\'"Z' --a x --b 2 --d y --e 3 --f 1 --g 2 ->  line4 = b'A\'"Z'  (RC=0; 0x22 stays literal)
  via line 2 as well: --b '3yj' (bytes 27 22) -> b'\'"' ; --b (bytes 27 09) -> b"'\t" ; --b (bytes 27 5c) -> b"'\\"

(d) Exhaustive proof of the complete short-escape set: I built a --b whose b58decode is all 256 bytes 0x00..0xff in order (348-char base58 string) and grepped line 2 for every backslash-plus-non-x pair:
  grep -o '\\[^x]' all256.got | sort | uniq -c  ->  1 \'   1 \\   1 \n   1 \r   1 \t
Exactly five short escapes across all 256 bytes. 158 \xNN escapes (29 C0 + 0x7f + 128 high). No \a \b \v \f \0 \e, and grep -o '\\[0-9]' over all my outputs matched NOTHING (no octal). Fresh C0 sweep i=1..31,127 with the byte ALONE (not A<byte>Z) reproduced their result: 0x07->b'\x07', 0x08->b'\x08', 0x09->b'\t', 0x0a->b'\n', 0x0b->b'\x0b', 0x0c->b'\x0c', 0x0d->b'\r', 0x1b->b'\x1b', 0x7f->b'\x7f', all RC=0.
verdicts.corrected_rule: The complete escape set for a bytes repr is: 0x09->\t, 0x0a->\n, 0x0d->\r, 0x5c->\\ (always), and 0x27->\' but ONLY when the delimiter is the single quote. Delimiter rule: use ' unless the bytes contain 0x27 AND NOT 0x22, in which case use " (so \" never appears, and an un-escaped 0x22 can sit inside a '-delimited repr, and an un-escaped 0x27 can sit inside a "-delimited repr). Every other byte with value < 0x20 or >= 0x7f uses \xNN; there are no \a \b \v \f \0 \e and no octal escapes. Bytes 0x20..0x7e other than 0x27/0x5c are emitted literally (space is NOT escaped: bytes 20 41 20 -> b' A ').

verdicts.rule: [2] Byte 0x00 renders as `\x00` — never `\0` — in leading, embedded, and all-zero positions. Leading zero bytes come from base58 '1' prefixes and are rendered the same as embedded ones.
verdicts.counterexample:
I tried hard to break it with trailing zeros, single-zero-only, digit-adjacent zeros, quote-adjacent zeros, and long zero runs. All fresh commands (all RC=0, all with --a x --c q --d y --e 3 --f 1 --g 2):
  --b '1'        -> line2 = b'\x00'            (single zero byte alone)
  --b '5wu'      -> b'A\x00'                   (TRAILING zero)
  --b 'NqKf'     -> b'A\x00B'
  --b '12fNHLj'  -> b'\x00A\x00B\x00'      (leading + embedded + trailing in one)
  --b '11111'    -> b'\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00'
  --b '1112UeoR' -> b'\x00\x00\x00\xff\x00\x00'
  --b '1A'       -> b'\x00\t'   --b '1B' -> b'\x00\n'   --b '15Q' -> b'\x00\xff'
  --b (bytes 00 27) -> b"\x00'"                (zero + quote-switch interaction: still \x00)
  --b '1'x40 (40 '1' chars) -> line2 is 164 bytes = 2 + 40*4 + 1 + 1, i.e. 40 x '\x00'
  --b (20 zeros then 30 30) -> b'\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x0000'
No `\0` ever: grep -o '\\[0-9]' over every output file matched nothing. od -c confirms the literal chars \ x 0 0.

IMPLEMENTATION DETAIL worth carrying over (does not refute the rule): because \xNN is always exactly two digits, a 0x00 followed by ASCII digits just concatenates - bytes [00,30] -> b'\x000' (--b '1q', od -c: b ' \ x 0 0 0 ') and bytes [00,30,30] -> b'\x0000' (--b '14fh'). A Node generator must not insert any separator, and a Node *parser* must consume exactly 2 hex digits.

verdicts.rule: [3] All 128 bytes 0x80-0xff render as `\x` + two lowercase hex digits, no exceptions, and the output contains the literal ASCII characters backslash, 'x', and the hex digits (not the raw high byte).
verdicts.counterexample:
I did NOT reuse their one giant string. Independent verification by three different routes:
(a) Per-byte sweep: for each i in 0x80..0xff I computed b58encode([i]) and ran
    /workspace/dataset/test20_executable --a x --b <b58> --c q --d y --e 3 --f 1 --g 2
  and compared line 2 against the literal b'\xNN'. 128/128 matched, all RC=0, zero mismatches.
(b) Different argument path - high bytes arriving through --c as UTF-8 (line 4 microscope):
    --c 'é'  -> b'\xc3\xa9'      --c '€' -> b'\xe2\x82\xac'
    --c '😀' -> b'\xf0\x9f\x98\x80'   --c 'ÿ' -> b'\xc3\xbf'
    --c $'a\té\xe2\x82\xac' -> b'a\t\xc3\xa9\xe2\x82\xac'   (all RC=0)
(c) No raw high byte on stdout: with --b decoding to [ff,fe,c3,a9], `sed -n 2p | od -c` gives  b ' \ x f f \ x f e \ x c 3 \ x a 9 ' \n , and `LC_ALL=C grep -c -P '[\x80-\xff]' full.out` returned 0 matches (rc=1) over the whole 12-line stdout.
(d) No truncation/ellipsis at length: a 600-byte payload (mixed high/low) produced a 1723-byte line 2 that matched my Node-modelled repr byte-for-byte via diff; grep for '...' found none.

CAVEAT the rule should mention (unverified only in the sense that it is about reachability, not rendering): high bytes can reach --a/--c/--d only as VALID UTF-8. A raw invalid byte in argv crashes:
  --c $'\xff'   -> RC=1, stdout empty, stderr: File "test20.py", line 17 ... UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\udcff' in position 0: surrogates not allowed
  --c $'A\x80B' -> RC=1, same error with '\udc80' in position 1

verdicts.rule: [4] Hex escapes are ALWAYS exactly two lowercase hex digits, zero-padded (\x00, \x0b, \x0f, \x1f, \x7f, \x8a, \xff). Uppercase hex never appears.
verdicts.counterexample:
Fresh exhaustive test rather than a sweep: --b set to the 348-char base58 of bytes 0x00..0xff in order.
  grep -o '\\x..' all256.got | wc -l          -> 158   (29 C0 + 0x7f + 128 high, exactly as expected)
  grep -o '\\x..' all256.got | grep '[A-F]' | wc -l -> 0   (no uppercase inside any escape)
  sorted-unique escapes run \x00,\x01,... through ...\xfc,\xfd,\xfe,\xff - all lowercase, all zero-padded to 2 digits
  diff against my Node model of the repr: IDENTICAL (739-byte line)
Zero-padding specifically re-verified in isolation: --b '1' -> b'\x00'; --c $'\x0b' -> b'\x0b'; --c $'\x0f' -> b'\x0f'; --c $'\x01' -> b'\x01'; --c $'\x7f' -> b'\x7f'.
Digit-adjacency does not widen an escape: bytes [8a,62] -> b'\x8ab' (od -c: b ' \ x 8 a b '), bytes [00,30] -> b'\x000'. Still exactly two digits.
